title: A Proof of the Kahn-Kalai Conjecture
authors: Jinyoung Park (Stanford University, USA), Huy Tuan Pham (Stanford University, USA)
abstract: Proving the "expectation-threshold" conjecture of Kahn and Kalai, we show that for any increasing property $\cF$ on a finite set $X$, \[p_c(\cF)=O(q(\cF)\log \ell(\cF)),\] where $p_c(\cF)$ and $q(\cF)$ are the threshold and "expectation threshold" of $\cF$, and $\ell(\cF)$ is the maximum size of a minimal member of $\cF$.

Abstract—Proving the “expectation-threshold” conjecture of
Kahn and Kalai, we show that for any increasing property F on
a ﬁnite set X,

Index Terms—monotone Boolean functions, thresholds,
expectation thresholds, random graphs

Roughly speaking, Theorem I.1 says that for any increasing
property, the threshold is always close to its trivial lower bound
given by the expectation threshold.
Thresholds have been a central subject in the study of
random discrete structures since its initiation by Erdős and
Rényi [5], [6]; the study of which has ﬂourished in random
graph theory, computer science [14], [21], and statistical
physics [10]. The deﬁnition of the threshold above is ﬁner
than the original Erdős-Rényi notion, according to which
p∗ = p∗ (n) is a threshold for F = Fn if μp (F) → 0

always an Erdős-Rényi threshold follows from [4], in which
it was observed that every increasing F admits a threshold
in the Erdős-Rényi sense. While much work has been done
identifying thresholds for speciﬁc properties (see [3], [11]),
another intensively studied direction in the study of thresholds
is “sharpness” of thresholds: we refer interested readers to [8],
[9].
To emphasize the strength of Theorem I.1, we point out
that, in [13], Kahn and Kalai write that “It would probably be
more sensible to conjecture that it is not true.” For example,
Theorem I.1 easily implies some very hard results on the
location of thresholds, for example, the appearance of perfect
matchings in random r-uniform hypergraphs [12], and the
appearance of a given bounded degree spanning tree in a
random graph [16]. For more discussion on the signiﬁcance
and applications of this theorem, we refer the readers to [7],
in which a weaker (“fractional”) version of Theorem I.1 is
proved.
Part of our proof is inspired by the algorithm and analysis
in breakthrough work on the sunﬂower conjecture [1], and
previous works on the fractional version of the theorem [7],
[15], though our implementation is signiﬁcantly different from
the ideas in those papers. In particular, our analysis completely
avoids the use of “spread,” which was a key ingredient in the
aforementioned papers. We also remove the need to separate
into pathological and non-pathological cases as in [7], [15].
The key object that we introduce is the “minimum fragment.”

The use of minimum fragments is inspired by our work
[18], where we resolve some conjectures and questions of
Talagrand on suprema of certain positive stochastic processes.
In particular, we prove Talagrand’s selector process conjecture
(raised in [21], [20] and [22]) and answer a question of
Talagrand about suprema of positive empirical processes
(raised in [20] and [23]). These give the ﬁrst known analogs
of Talagrand’s celebrated results on suprema of Gaussian
processes in the setting of general positive empirical processes
and selector processes.
